newsitem.title: INDIA: Shaky Indian shares seen having a long way to go.
newsitem.headline: Shaky Indian shares seen having a long way to go.

text.p: Troubled Indian stock markets bounced back in early afternoon trade on Tuesday after plunging for the second straight day, but analysts said they saw little prospect of a strong rebound in the near-term.
"One could expect some kind of correction, but the market will stay down for some time," said Alok Sethi, director at Natwest Markets, the investment arm of National Westminister Bank Plc.
The 30-share index of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) was up 18.48 points at 3,021.34 in the early afternoon after having tumbled to 2,930.93 in early Tuesday deals.
The index fell 98.41 points, or 3.17 percent, on Monday after plunging 153.46 points, or 4.71 percent, last week.
Analysts attribute the drop to an economic slowdown that will hit corporate earnings growth in 1996/97 (April-March), compounded by political uncertainties.
"We think there's still some way to go for a valuation of the market relative to interest rates," said Devina Mehra, director at broking firm First Global Investments.
"It's not even fairly valued...forget being undervalued."
She saw the benchmark BSE index sliding to 2,200-2,400 for a strong rebound to get going.
"That's the level when you could expect strong buying to come in...a bull phase," she said.
Mehra said risk-free term deposits with banks offered upwards of 14 percent annually while other debt instruments gave a return of 17-20 percent.

"Investments in equity must give a return of more than 24 percent to lure buyers," she said, adding that top stocks like Tata Iron and Steel Company, Ranbaxy Laboratories and Hindalco Industries were currently overpriced.
After two years of robust growth, the Indian economy is widely seen to be slowing this year.
"I won't call it recession," Mehra said. "A slowdown? Yes."

India's index of industrial production grew slower at 6.8 percent year-on-year in June, the latest month for which figures are available, against 10.6 percent in May and compared with 12.2 percent in June 1995.
Analysts expect automobile, software, pharmaceuticals, hotels and consumer goods firms to do well, with the capital goods segment, steel, cement and petrochemicals staying down.
They said easier liquidity conditions had not helped companies because interest rates had remained high and the depressed primary markets made it impossible to raise funds.
Natwest's Sethi said a "regular supply of paper" by Indian firms through the issue of global depositary receipts (GDRs) was another factor that contributed to the stocks slide.
Last week the State Bank of India (SBI), the country's largest commercial bank, mopped up $370 million through GDRs.

Other big issues in the past three months were by Tata Engineering and Locomotive Company, India's biggest truckmaker, and finance firm Industrial Credit and Investment Corp of India, both raising $200 million.
Sethi said it was incorrect to say that foreign institutional investors (FIIs) were behind the downside.
"We seem to blame the FIIs a lot," he said. "That's not the case. It's the lack of demand from domestic funds and retail investors."
